## Abstract

We classified webpages based on whether there was evidence of fraud or other crime using text extracted from headings and paragraphs from scraped HTML pages. After preprocessing, word-level text was represented by term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features. A two-hidden-layer neural network achieved **83.6%** testing accuracy for binary classification; a separate neural network achieved **77.9%** testing accuracy on multiclass classification.

## Preprocessing

Using `rvest`, we extracted only HTML headings (`<h1>`–`<h6>`) and paragraphs (`<p>`) and combined their text. The `parse_fn` cleaner removed URLs, emails, apostrophes, punctuation, numbers, symbols, and `nbsp` artifacts, separated joined lowercase/uppercase words, converted text to lowercase, and normalized whitespace.  HTMLs that were filtered out in preprocessing were assigned an empty string to represent their cleaned text. The function `nlp_fn` handled removal of stop words, lemmatization of words, and exclusion of words with two or fewer characters. After the HTMLs were cleaned, they were tokenized into unigrams and the term frequencies and inverse document frequencies were calculated. Values were then multiplied to create a TF-IDF matrix as the quantitative representation for the model. The 7,500 most frequent unigrams were used for binary classification and 10,000 most frequent unigrams for multiclass classification subject to selection only if they appear in at least two HTMLs and in fewer than 90% of training documents. Training vocabularies and IDF weights were applied to the test data to calculate their TF-IDF values.

## Methods

### Binary Classification 

We trained a feedforward neural network with two hidden layers of 20 neurons with ReLU activation each. Minimal L2 regularization was applied at each hidden layer and a single output neuron with sigmoid activation provided the probability for classifying claim content as relevant or irrelevant. Training used the Adam optimizer and binary cross-entropy loss for 20 epochs. An 80/20 train-test split stratified by class and five-fold cross-validation on the training portion supported model selection. Direct TF-IDF inputs were found to perform better than the PCA-based alternatives examined. Many hyperparameters like the number of neurons in each layer, the number of hidden layers, regularization amounts, and activation functions were tested before settling on the ones found. 

### Multiclass Classification

A separate neural network predicted one of five claim-content categories using two hidden layers of 30 neurons with ReLU activation each. L2 regularization with a parameter of 0.001 was applied to each hidden layer. 5 neurons with in the output layer with softmax activation to provide probabilities for each category. It was trained for 20 epochs with the Adam optimizer and the sparse categorical cross-entropy loss function. To address class imbalances in the data such as the category "Other claim content" only making up around 4% of training data, class weights were added to the model to help with training and prediction. We used a 80/20 split stratified by class and five-fold cross-validation for model evaluation. The final model increased the minimum document frequency to three for token selection compared to the binary model.


## Results
Metrics were calculated on a held-out test set of data. 429 webpages were used in binary classification and 430 webpages were used in multiclass classification. The positive class for binary classification is "Relevant Claim Content."

**Binary Classification Metrics** 

| Sensitivity | Specificity | Accuracy | ROC AUC |
|:-----------:|:-----------:|:--------:|:-------:|
| 83.5% | 83.8% | **83.6%** | 89.0% |

**Multiclass Classification Metrics** 

| Macro Sensitivity | Macro Specificity | Accuracy | Macro F1 |
|:-----------------:|:-----------------:|:--------:|:--------:|
| 74.9% | 93.6% | **77.9%** | 74.0% |

> Multiclass sensitivity was highest for *Possible Fatality* (88.6%) and lowest for *Other claim content* (54.2%). Sensitivity and specificity for multiclass results use equally weighted one-versus-rest averages across the five categories. Accuracy is the overall fraction correctly classified.
